question: MARPOL Annex I covers pollution by:
explanation: Annex I: oil; II: noxious liquid substances in bulk; III: harmful packaged substances; IV: sewage; V: garbage; VI: air pollution.

question: MARPOL Annex V regulates:
explanation: Annex V generally prohibits discharge of garbage at sea, with limited exceptions such as food waste beyond set distances.

question: Outside special areas, an oil tanker may discharge oily cargo residue only if, among other conditions, the instantaneous rate does not exceed:
explanation: The tanker must also be more than 50 NM from land, en route, with ODME in operation, and the total discharged must be within the permitted fraction of cargo.

question: Oil Record Book Part II on tankers records:
explanation: Part I covers machinery space operations on all ships.

question: Since 1 January 2020, the global limit on fuel oil sulphur content outside ECAs is:
explanation: Inside SOx Emission Control Areas the limit is 0.10% m/m, unless an approved equivalent such as a scrubber is used.

question: Discharge of plastics into the sea is:
explanation: MARPOL Annex V bans plastics at sea, including synthetic ropes, nets and plastic garbage bags.

question: Outside special areas, comminuted food waste (25 mm or less) may be discharged no closer to the nearest land than:
explanation: Food waste that has not been comminuted needs at least 12 NM. Special areas have stricter rules.

question: The D-2 standard of the Ballast Water Management Convention is a:
options: Performance standard limiting viable organisms in discharged ballast water
Ballast exchange standard requiring 95% volumetric exchange
explanation: D-1 is ballast water exchange. D-2 is normally met with an approved treatment system.

question: SOPEP stands for:
options: Standard Oil Pumping and Emptying Plan
explanation: Required by MARPOL Annex I for oil tankers of 150 GT and above and other ships of 400 GT and above.

question: The Garbage Record Book must be kept on board for at least:
options: Two years after the last entry
explanation: Entries include date, time, position, garbage category and estimated amount discharged or incinerated.

question: MARPOL Annex IV covers:
explanation: Annex IV regulates sewage discharge and requires approved treatment plants, comminuting systems or holding tanks.

question: Oil Record Books must be kept on board, readily available for inspection, for:
options: Three years after the last entry
explanation: Each completed operation is signed by the officer in charge and each page by the master.

question: CII, introduced under MARPOL Annex VI, stands for:
explanation: Ships are rated A-E each year based on operational CO2 emissions per transport work.

question: Under MARPOL Annex VI, new installations containing ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs are:
explanation: HCFCs were allowed in new installations only until 1 January 2020.

question: The Ballast Water Record Book must record:
options: Each ballast uptake, treatment, exchange and discharge, with dates, positions and volumes
explanation: The ship must also carry an approved Ballast Water Management Plan.

question: Noxious liquid substances carried in bulk, such as many chemicals, are regulated by MARPOL Annex:
explanation: Annex II applies mainly to chemical tankers and divides substances into categories X, Y, Z and OS.

question: Which MARPOL Annex regulates harmful substances carried by sea in packaged form?
explanation: Packaged harmful substances, including marine pollutants under the IMDG Code, must be properly packed, marked and stowed.

question: Air pollution and the energy efficiency of ships are regulated by:
explanation: Annex VI controls SOx, NOx, ozone-depleting substances, VOCs, incineration and greenhouse gas measures such as EEXI and CII.

question: MARPOL is a convention of the:
explanation: MARPOL was adopted in 1973 and modified by the 1978 Protocol, hence 'MARPOL 73/78'.

question: Under MARPOL Annex V, garbage placards informing crew of the discharge rules must be displayed on every ship of:
explanation: Placards must be in the working language of the crew and, for international voyages, also in English, French or Spanish.

question: A Garbage Management Plan is required on every ship of:
options: 100 GT and above, and every ship certified to carry 15 or more persons
500 GT and above that carry passengers
explanation: The plan names the person responsible and sets procedures for collecting, storing, processing and disposing of garbage.

question: A Garbage Record Book is required on ships of:
options: 400 GT and above, and ships certified to carry 15 or more persons on international voyages
explanation: Each discharge, incineration or delivery ashore is recorded with date, time, position, category and estimated amount.

question: Under MARPOL Annex V, discharging used cooking oil into the sea is:
options: Allowed more than 12 nautical miles from land
Allowed if it is mixed with water
explanation: Cooking oil is a separate garbage category and must be delivered ashore or otherwise disposed of properly.

question: Outside special areas, food waste that has NOT been comminuted may be discharged only en route and at least:
options: 1 nautical mile from the nearest land
3 nautical miles from the nearest land
12 nautical miles from the nearest land
200 nautical miles from the nearest land
explanation: Comminuted food waste (25 mm or less) may be discharged from 3 nautical miles.

question: In the Mediterranean Sea special area, food waste may be discharged only when the ship is en route and:
options: It is at least 3 nautical miles from land, without comminuting
It has been comminuted to 25 mm or less and the ship is at least 12 nautical miles from the nearest land
At any distance if the waste is bagged
explanation: Special areas have stricter garbage discharge rules than other sea areas.

question: Which of these is a MARPOL Annex V special area?
explanation: Annex V special areas also include the Mediterranean, Baltic, Black Sea, Red Sea, Gulfs area, Wider Caribbean and Antarctic.

question: Inside a SOx Emission Control Area, the sulphur content of fuel oil used must not exceed:
explanation: An approved equivalent such as an exhaust gas cleaning system may be used instead of compliant fuel.

question: Since 1 May 2025, which sea area has been added as a SOx Emission Control Area under MARPOL Annex VI?
explanation: Existing SOx ECAs include the Baltic, the North Sea, the North American area and the US Caribbean area.

question: Under MARPOL Annex V, ashes from the shipboard incinerator may be:
options: Delivered to a port reception facility; their discharge into the sea is not permitted
Discharged more than 3 nautical miles from land
Mixed with food waste and discharged
explanation: Incinerator ashes are a separate garbage category and may contain toxic or plastic residues.

question: Since 1 March 2020, a ship without an approved exhaust gas cleaning system may not:
options: Carry fuel oil with more than 0.50% sulphur for combustion purposes
explanation: This 'carriage ban' supports enforcement of the global 0.50% sulphur limit.

question: Under MARPOL Annex VI, bunker delivery notes must be kept on board for at least:
explanation: The BDN shows the quantity, density and sulphur content of the fuel and is accompanied by a sealed sample.

question: An IOPP Certificate is required for oil tankers of 150 GT and above and for other ships of:
explanation: Its supplement (Form A for non-tankers, Form B for oil tankers) records the ship's pollution prevention equipment.

question: A Shipboard Marine Pollution Emergency Plan (SMPEP) is a plan that:
options: Is required only for passenger ships
Covers both oil and noxious liquid substance pollution incidents in one document
explanation: Ships carrying noxious liquid substances may combine their SOPEP and NLS plan into an SMPEP.

question: For an oil tanker delivered after 1979, the total quantity of oil discharged into the sea on a ballast voyage must not exceed:
options: 1/30,000 of the total quantity of the cargo of which the residue formed a part
explanation: This is one of the conditions for discharge from the cargo area outside special areas.

question: Outside special areas, how far from the nearest land must an oil tanker be before discharging oily mixtures from her cargo area?
explanation: She must also be en route, within the instantaneous rate limit, with the ODME and slop tank arrangements working.

question: The Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System (ODME) on a tanker:
options: Measures the oil content of the fuel
Monitors and records discharges of oily ballast and stops them automatically if the limits are exceeded
explanation: Its records must be kept for at least three years.

question: On an oil tanker, slop tanks are used to:
options: Store lubricating oil for the engine
Collect tank washings and oily residues so that the oil can separate from the water
explanation: The 'load on top' method allows separated oil to be retained and loaded with the next cargo.

question: Segregated ballast tanks (SBT) on a tanker are:
options: Tanks used only for ballast and completely separated from the cargo oil and fuel oil systems
Cargo tanks that sometimes carry ballast
explanation: Ballast in SBT never contacts oil, so it can be discharged without oily pollution.

question: Under MARPOL Annex I, double hulls are required for oil tankers of 5,000 tonnes deadweight and above delivered on or after:
explanation: Single-hull tankers were phased out under later amendments.

question: Under MARPOL Annex II, noxious liquid substances that present a major hazard to marine resources or human health are classed as Category:
explanation: Category X substances are prohibited from discharge into the sea; Y and Z are less hazardous; OS means other substances.

question: On a chemical tanker, operations with noxious liquid substances are recorded in the:
explanation: Loading, transfer, discharge, tank washing and discharge of residues must all be recorded.

question: After unloading a Category X substance, the tank must be:
options: Prewashed before the ship leaves the port of unloading, with the residues delivered to a reception facility
Washed at sea and the washings discharged at any distance
Left unwashed until the next loading port
Filled with sea water ballast only
explanation: The prewash continues until the concentration of the substance in the effluent meets the required limit, as verified by a surveyor.

question: Under MARPOL Annex IV, sewage that has not been comminuted or disinfected may be discharged only when the ship is:
options: More than 3 nautical miles from land at any speed
More than 12 nautical miles from the nearest land, en route at not less than 4 knots, at a moderate rate
explanation: Comminuted and disinfected sewage may be discharged more than 3 nautical miles from land.

question: Effluent from an approved sewage treatment plant may be discharged:
options: Only more than 200 miles from land
Without distance restrictions, provided it shows no visible floating solids or discolouration of the water
explanation: Stricter rules apply to passenger ships in the Baltic Sea special area.

question: Grey water on board, such as drainage from showers, sinks and laundries, is:
options: Classed as Category X under Annex II
Prohibited from discharge everywhere under Annex V
Not considered sewage under MARPOL Annex IV
Treated as oily water under Annex I
explanation: Sewage means drainage from toilets, medical premises, spaces with live animals, or water mixed with these.

question: The D-1 ballast water exchange standard requires ships performing exchange to achieve at least:
options: 95% volumetric exchange of the ballast water
explanation: D-1 is being replaced by the D-2 performance standard as ships install treatment systems.

question: Where possible, ballast water exchange under D-1 should be carried out:
options: Within 12 nautical miles of the port of arrival
In water less than 50 m deep
At least 200 nautical miles from the nearest land, in water at least 200 m deep
explanation: If that is not possible, at least 50 nautical miles from land in water at least 200 m deep.

question: When the pumping-through method is used for ballast water exchange, pumping three times the volume of each tank is considered to meet:
options: The tank cleaning standard for Annex II
explanation: Less than three times may be accepted if the ship can show at least 95% exchange.

question: Under the Ballast Water Management Convention, ships must carry:
options: An approved Ballast Water Management Plan and a Ballast Water Record Book
explanation: Ships of 400 GT and above also need an International Ballast Water Management Certificate.

question: The main purpose of the Ballast Water Management Convention is to:
options: Limit the amount of cargo carried
Prevent the spread of harmful aquatic organisms and pathogens carried in ballast water
explanation: Invasive species moved in ballast can seriously damage local ecosystems, health and economies.

question: The AFS Convention prohibits the use on ships' hulls of anti-fouling paints containing:
explanation: TBT harmed shellfish and marine life; cybutryne was later also banned.

question: The Hong Kong Convention, which entered into force in June 2025, deals with:
options: Safe and environmentally sound recycling of ships
explanation: Ships must carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials identifying materials such as asbestos and PCBs.

question: The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) is:
options: An annual operational rating from A to E
A one-time technical measure of an existing ship's design energy efficiency
explanation: Ships that do not meet the required EEXI may use measures such as engine power limitation.

question: SEEMP stands for:
options: Safety Equipment and Emergency Maintenance Plan
explanation: The SEEMP includes the methods for collecting fuel data and the plan to meet the required CII.

question: Under the CII regulations, a ship rated D for three consecutive years, or rated E in one year, must:
options: Develop a corrective action plan as part of her SEEMP
explanation: Ratings run from A (best) to E; the required CII becomes stricter each year.

question: The IMO Data Collection System requires ships of 5,000 GT and above to:
options: Collect and report their annual fuel oil consumption to their flag Administration
explanation: The data, including distance travelled and hours under way, is used for CII ratings and IMO analysis.

question: The CLC Convention (Civil Liability Convention) deals with:
options: The shipowner's liability for oil pollution damage from tankers carrying persistent oil as cargo
explanation: Ships carrying more than 2,000 t of oil in bulk as cargo must carry a certificate of insurance.

question: Pollution damage caused by fuel oil from a ship that is not a tanker is covered by the:
explanation: Registered owners of ships over 1,000 GT must hold insurance and carry a certificate.

question: If oil is spilled into the sea from your ship, the incident must be:
options: Reported only at the end of the voyage
Recorded only in the deck log
Reported without delay to the nearest coastal state, as set out in the SOPEP
explanation: MARPOL Protocol I requires reports of discharges or probable discharges of harmful substances.

question: During bunkering, deck scuppers are plugged in order to:
options: Contain any oil spilled on deck so it does not go overboard
explanation: Spill equipment such as absorbents, pumps and drip trays should also be ready at the manifold.

question: In the Garbage Record Book, garbage Category A is:
explanation: Other categories include B food wastes, C domestic wastes, D cooking oil, E incinerator ashes and F operational wastes.

question: Under MARPOL Annex VI, a VOC management plan is required on:
explanation: The plan describes how vapour emissions of volatile organic compounds are minimised during loading, voyage and discharge.

question: Under MARPOL, port states must provide:
options: Adequate reception facilities for ships' waste without causing undue delay
explanation: Inadequate facilities can be reported to IMO through the flag state.

question: Under MARPOL Annex V, synthetic ropes and fishing nets are treated as:
options: Domestic waste that may be thrown overboard
Plastics, which may not be discharged into the sea
explanation: Plastics include all garbage containing or made of plastic in any form.

question: Under MARPOL Annex VI, shipboard incineration of PVC (polyvinyl chlorides) is:
options: Prohibited, except in incinerators type-approved for burning it
Allowed if mixed with food waste
explanation: Annex VI also prohibits incinerating Annex I, II and III cargo residues and contaminated packing materials.
